lead: This unit turns a real machine into a dot and a set of arrows. You learn to replace forces by vectors, add them into one resultant, draw a free body diagram, and set the sum to zero — in a plane and in space. After it you can find unknown tensions and reactions for any particle, with the units to prove it.
about: The unit starts in 1.1 with the idealizations that make mechanics solvable — the particle, the rigid body, the point force — and with Newton's laws and SI units. Chapter 1.2 treats force as a vector and builds the algebra of addition, dot and cross products. Chapter 1.3 splits one force into components along chosen directions; 1.4 reverses it and adds any number of concurrent forces into one resultant. Chapter 1.5 turns a real support into a free body diagram, and 1.6 sets the vector sum to zero, which for three coplanar forces is Lami's theorem. Chapter 1.7 repeats both steps in three dimensions, where each force brings three components and equilibrium three equations. Every chapter ends where the next begins: a diagram produces equations, equations produce unknown forces.

chapters.idea: Real machines are too complex to solve directly, so mechanics replaces them by ideal models — particle, rigid body — and then applies Newton's laws with consistent units.
chapters.depth: Scope of engineering mechanics; the split into statics (bodies at rest) and dynamics (bodies in motion), and dynamics into kinematics (geometry of motion) and kinetics (forces that cause it). Fundamental quantities: length, mass, time, force. Newton's three laws, plus the gravitation law that gives W = mg. Idealizations: particle, rigid body, continuum, line of action of a force. SI base and derived units, prefixes, the kgf, and g = 9.81 m/s². Homogeneity of an equation as a unit check. Some syllabi call this 'fundamental concepts and principles of engineering mechanics' or 'introduction and idealizations of mechanics'.

figure.title: From a real body to a solvable model
figure.aria: A flowchart shows a real body replaced either by a particle or by a rigid body, then solved with Newton's laws and SI units to reach an answer in newtons.

chapters.example: A 25 kg sack of rice hangs from a single rope. Take g = 9.81 m/s². (a) Find the weight of the sack in N and in kgf. (b) The rope is rated for 300 N — is it safe? (c) Check whether v² = u² + 2as is homogeneous in SI units. Answer: W = 25 × 9.81 = 245.25 N, which is 245.25 ÷ 9.81 = 25 kgf. Since 245.25 N < 300 N the rope is safe. Both sides of v² = u² + 2as carry m²/s², so the equation is homogeneous.
chapters.trap: Writing 25 kg as the answer for weight, and mixing kgf with N inside one equation.
chapters.leave: Motion of a particle under forces (Unit 5); stress and deformation of real bodies (later subject).

chapters.idea: A force is a vector: it has magnitude and direction, and vectors add by the triangle or parallelogram law, never by adding their sizes.
chapters.depth: Scalar and vector quantities with examples from mechanics; notation; equality and equivalence of vectors (two forces are equivalent when magnitude and direction match, not position); unit vector; position vector of a point. Addition by triangle law, subtraction as adding the negative, multiplication by a scalar. Dot product A·B = AB cos θ (a scalar) and cross product |A×B| = AB sin θ (a vector, right-hand rule). i, j, k components, magnitude √(Ax² + Ay² + Az²), and the angle between two vectors from cos θ = A·B/(AB). Some syllabi call this 'vector approach to addition and subtraction of forces' or 'elements of vector algebra'.

figure.aria: A tree puts vector algebra into three branches: addition with the triangle, parallelogram and subtraction rules, the scalar dot product, and the vector cross product.

chapters.example: F₁ = 3i + 4j N and F₂ = 4i + 3j N act at a point. Find F₁ + F₂, F₁ − F₂, F₁·F₂, F₁×F₂ and the angle between them. Answer: F₁ + F₂ = 7i + 7j N, magnitude 7√2 = 9.90 N at 45° to the x-axis. F₁ − F₂ = −i + j N, magnitude 1.41 N at 135°. F₁·F₂ = 12 + 12 = 24 N². |F₁| = |F₂| = 5 N, so cos θ = 24/25 = 0.96 and θ = 16.3°. F₁×F₂ = (3×3 − 4×4)k = −7k N², i.e. 7 N² into the page; check 5 × 5 × sin 16.3° = 7.
chapters.trap: Adding magnitudes (3 + 4 = 7 N) instead of components, and writing a vector answer as a bare number with no direction.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1 (force as a quantity, units, the particle model).
chapters.leave: Moment of a force as r × F (Unit 2); differentiation of vectors for velocity and acceleration (Unit 5).

chapters.idea: One force can be replaced by two or more forces that add up to it — resolution — and the reverse, composition, rebuilds the single force from them.
chapters.depth: Rectangular resolution Fx = F cos θ and Fy = F sin θ, with θ measured from the positive x-axis and the sign taken from the quadrant. Worked habits: draw the force, mark θ, decide the signs before substituting. Oblique resolution along two directions that are not at right angles, using the sine rule on the force triangle. Composition of two forces by the parallelogram law: R = √(P² + Q² + 2PQ cos α) and tan θ = Q sin α/(P + Q cos α), θ measured from P; check the special cases α = 0° (R = P + Q), α = 90° (R = √(P² + Q²)), α = 180° (R = |P − Q|). Some syllabi call composition 'resultant of two forces' and resolution 'splitting a force into components'.

figure.aria: Two curves show the horizontal and vertical components of a 50 N force as its angle turns through a full circle; each component peaks at 50 N and falls to zero or −50 N a quarter turn later.

chapters.example: A force of 50 N acts at 30° above the horizontal. (a) Resolve it into horizontal and vertical components. (b) Resolve the same force along the horizontal and along a direction at 75° above the horizontal. Answer: (a) Fx = 50 cos 30° = 43.3 N, Fy = 50 sin 30° = 25.0 N. (b) The angle between the force and the horizontal is 30°, between the force and the 75° line is 45°, and between the two chosen directions is 75°. By the sine rule P/sin 45° = Q/sin 30° = 50/sin 75°, so P = 36.6 N along the horizontal and Q = 25.9 N along 75°. Check: 36.6i + 25.9(cos 75° i + sin 75° j) = 43.3i + 25.0j N, the original force.
chapters.trap: Using cos for the wrong axis after measuring θ from the vertical, and dropping the minus sign when the force points into the second or third quadrant.
chapters.leave: Resultant of three or more forces (Chapter 4); splitting a reaction into normal and friction parts (Unit 3).

chapters.idea: For forces meeting at one point the resultant is simply the vector sum: add all x components, add all y components, then rebuild one force from the two totals.
chapters.depth: Analytical method: fix a sign convention, write each force as (F cos θ)i + (F sin θ)j, sum to get Rx = ΣFx and Ry = ΣFy, then R = √(Rx² + Ry²) and θ = tan⁻¹(Ry/Rx) corrected for the quadrant (add 180° when Rx < 0). Graphical check by the force polygon drawn tip to tail in any order; a closed polygon means R = 0. Special cases: collinear forces, two forces at an angle, equal forces equally spaced summing to zero. Common exam wording: 'determine the resultant of the given coplanar concurrent force system and its direction with the x-axis'. Some syllabi call this 'resultant of several concurrent forces in a plane'.

figure.aria: A force polygon drawn tip to tail with the four given forces; the single arrow from the start point O to the last tip E is the 95.4 N resultant.

chapters.example: Four ropes pull on a ring at O. F₁ = 60 N at 0°, F₂ = 100 N at 60°, F₃ = 75 N at 150°, F₄ = 40 N at 270°, all angles anticlockwise from +x. Find the resultant. Answer: ΣFx = 60 + 100 cos 60° + 75 cos 150° + 40 cos 270° = 60 + 50 − 65.0 + 0 = 45.0 N. ΣFy = 0 + 100 sin 60° + 75 sin 150° + 40 sin 270° = 0 + 86.6 + 37.5 − 40 = 84.1 N. R = √(45.0² + 84.1²) = 95.4 N, at θ = tan⁻¹(84.1/45.0) = 61.9° above +x, in the first quadrant.
chapters.trap: Writing θ = tan⁻¹(Ry/Rx) straight from the calculator when Rx is negative; the resultant then comes out 180° wrong.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2 and 3 (vector components, resolution, parallelogram law).
chapters.leave: Non-concurrent force systems, force–couple reduction and equivalent force systems (Unit 2).

chapters.idea: Cut the body free of its supports, draw only the external forces acting on it, and the mechanics problem becomes a picture you can write equations from.
chapters.depth: Why the diagram exists: equilibrium equations talk about forces on one body, so every other body must be removed and replaced by the force it exerts. Steps: choose the body (or the knot), isolate it, mark weight W = mg vertically down at the centroid, replace each support by the reaction it can give (normal to a smooth surface, tension along a rope or cable, two components at a pin), add applied loads, then check each arrow has a known source. Internal forces and forces the body exerts on others never appear — action and reaction sit on different diagrams. Inclined surfaces: the normal is perpendicular to the surface, not vertical. Support types are named only in passing; the full table and rigid-body diagrams are Unit 2. Some syllabi list 'concept of free body diagram' as a separate exam question.

figure.aria: A five-step flowchart: choose the body, cut it free, add the weight, replace each support by a reaction, add ropes and loads, then count the arrows.

chapters.example: A block of mass 10 kg rests on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal and is held from sliding by a string parallel to the plane. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Draw the free body diagram and find the tension and the normal reaction. Answer: three forces act on the block — weight W = 10 × 9.81 = 98.1 N vertically down, normal reaction N perpendicular to the plane, tension T up the plane. Take axes along and perpendicular to the plane. Along the plane: T − 98.1 sin 30° = 0, so T = 49.05 N. Perpendicular to the plane: N − 98.1 cos 30° = 0, so N = 84.96 N.
chapters.trap: Drawing the force the block presses on the plane (that acts on the plane, not on the block), and putting W along the incline instead of vertically down.
chapters.leave: The full support and reaction table, and free body diagrams of rigid bodies (Unit 2); friction forces on the incline (Unit 3).

chapters.idea: A particle is in equilibrium when the forces on it add to zero, and when there are exactly three coplanar forces that zero sum can be written as Lami's theorem.
chapters.depth: Condition ΣF = 0, written for a plane system as ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0, which fixes at most two unknowns. Order of work: free body diagram first, axes next, equations last. Lami's theorem: if exactly three concurrent coplanar forces P, Q, R keep a particle in equilibrium, then P/sin α = Q/sin β = R/sin γ, where α is the angle between Q and R, β between P and R, γ between P and Q. Proof from the closed force triangle and the sine rule. Limits: exactly three forces, all through one point; with four or more, use the two component equations. Choose Lami when the angles are given directly and the triangle is awkward; choose components when forces are along axes. Some syllabi write the topic as 'equilibrium of a particle, Lami's theorem and problems'.

figure.aria: Three forces meet at knot O: a 50 N string up to the left at 150°, an 86.6 N string up to the right at 60°, and a 100 N weight hanging straight down.

chapters.example: A lamp of weight 100 N hangs from a knot O. String OA makes 30° above the horizontal to the left, string OB makes 60° above the horizontal to the right. Find the two tensions. Answer: the angle between the strings is 180° − 30° − 60° = 90°; between T₁ and W is 120°; between T₂ and W is 150°. By Lami, T₁/sin 150° = T₂/sin 120° = 100/sin 90°. So T₁ = 100 × 0.5 = 50 N and T₂ = 100 × 0.866 = 86.6 N. Check with components: ΣFx = 86.6 cos 60° − 50 cos 30° = 43.3 − 43.3 = 0; ΣFy = 86.6 sin 60° + 50 sin 30° − 100 = 75 + 25 − 100 = 0.
chapters.trap: Dividing a force by the sine of an angle beside it instead of the angle between the other two forces, and applying Lami to four forces.
chapters.leave: Equilibrium of a rigid body with moments (Unit 2); equilibrium with friction (Unit 3); D'Alembert's principle for moving bodies (Unit 5).

chapters.idea: In space a force has three components, so equilibrium gives three equations and a resultant needs direction cosines, not one plane angle.
chapters.depth: Three-dimensional Cartesian frame with the right-hand rule. Force along a line: r = (x₂−x₁)i + (y₂−y₁)j + (z₂−z₁)k, magnitude |r| = √(rx² + ry² + rz²), unit vector n̂ = r/|r|, and F = F n̂, with F the magnitude of the force. Components Fx = F cos θx and direction cosines cos θx = rx/|r|, cos θy, cos θz, satisfying cos²θx + cos²θy + cos²θz = 1. Resultant R = √(Rx² + Ry² + Rz²) with cos θx = Rx/R. Equilibrium: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣFz = 0, at most three unknowns; cables carry tension along their own lines. Only a few universities ask for three-dimensional support reactions here; the standard treatment belongs to Unit 2. Some syllabi call this 'addition of concurrent forces in space' and 'equilibrium of a particle in space'.

figure.aria: A flowchart from the coordinates of two points to the vector AB, its length and unit vector, the force vector, the three equilibrium sums and the solved unknowns.

chapters.example: A force of 260 N acts along the line from A(1, 2, 0) m to B(4, 6, 12) m. (a) Write it as a vector and give its direction cosines. (b) A particle at A also carries a force of 130 N along the line from A to C(5, −10, 3) m; find the resultant. (c) What third force keeps the particle in equilibrium? Answer: (a) AB = 3i + 4j + 12k m, |AB| = √(9 + 16 + 144) = 13 m, so F₁ = (260/13)(3i + 4j + 12k) = 60i + 80j + 240k N, with direction cosines 0.231, 0.308, 0.923. (b) AC = 4i − 12j + 3k m, |AC| = 13 m, so F₂ = (130/13)(4i − 12j + 3k) = 40i − 120j + 30k N. R = 100i − 40j + 270k N, |R| = √(10000 + 1600 + 72900) = 290.7 N. (c) The equilibrant is −R = −100i + 40j − 270k N, also of magnitude 290.7 N.
chapters.trap: Using the raw coordinate differences as components without dividing by |AB|, and taking the direction B to A when the force is stated from A to B.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 2, 3, 5 and 6 (vector algebra, resolution, free body diagram, equilibrium conditions).
chapters.leave: Moments and couples in three dimensions, and rigid-body equilibrium in space (Unit 2).
